The user attended Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI), chose WPI for its project-based education and academic rigor, and majored in Biomedical Engineering. The user describes WPI as a place where they grew personally and academically, moving from a high school senior with big dreams to a capable researcher. WPI coursework required learning material and applying it in projects; skills gained included biomedical engineering design, cell passaging, circuit design, and fabrication. The user especially valued support from WPI staff and professors and hopes to continue growing at WPI while helping others as they were helped.

The user is highly interested in neural interfaces and hopes eventually to start a research company developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) to treat neurological disorders and enhance the human brain. The user’s research ambitions shifted while at WPI, but this central interest remained consistent.

In 2020, the user was accepted into a summer undergraduate research program in Computational Neuroscience hosted by Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh. Despite the coronavirus pandemic and lacking formal training in neuroscience and independent research, the user prepared independently and succeeded in a research environment. The user worked in Dr. Aaron Batista’s lab, guided by graduate student Erinn Grigsby, studying how neuron dropping affected decoder performance. Using Matlab skills learned at WPI, the user and another student created three Kalman filters and linear regression decoders, with different position, velocity, and velocity-position decoder configurations, to test which decoder was most robust. The experience developed the user’s ability to find relevant information in research papers, formulate questions, identify objective ways to answer them, and understand and design brain-computer-interface decoders.

At WPI, the user completed an MQP project led by Professor Dirk Albrecht. The user’s group designed a programmable electrical stimulator to study deep brain stimulation in C. elegans worms. Despite the challenges of remote learning, the project produced results that raised further questions, which the user hoped to pursue in graduate studies at WPI. The work required the user to develop as an engineer and researcher, understand problems, and find solutions quickly. The user learned COMSOL analysis and microfluidic device fabrication and refined laboratory experience.

The user’s academic plan is to earn a master’s degree in Neuroscience and a Ph.D. in Biomedical Engineering with a concentration in neuroscience at WPI. After completing the Ph.D., the user plans to start a research company dedicated to designing and building minimally invasive, high-resolution, bidirectional neural interfaces. The user recognizes that substantial scientific advances are needed to make such devices feasible and hopes to contribute to those advances, mentor the next generation, and help others answer questions about the world.
